To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have demonstrated a wearable eye tracking system that can operate robustly in the real world and can trade off power for accuracy.

a) we propose a new architecture that enables a wearable eye tracker to operate robustly in the natural environment by switching models based on the illumination, b) we demonstrate the power--robustrness tradeoffs inherent to the design of a real-world wearable eye tracker, c) our system operates at power levels of 7mW, or 32mW, and achieves error of 0.6O in estimating pupil center, and 0.22mm in estimating pupil diameter.
we propose a novel staged architecture for an eye tracker that enables robustness-power tradeoffs in a wearable setting, and demonstrate the feasibility of such a design.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the design of a system that can continuously measure the human eye in the real world, and we believe that the techniques developed in this work will have a broad impact in the design of wearable devices.
enabling a wearable system to adapt gracefully to a variety of environments, and to do so with a minimal power penalty, and with minimal user effort in training the model.

the design and implementation of a wearable system that enables robust eye tracking in the natural environment, while minimizing the impact on the user in terms of power consumption, training effort, and user attention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our system can track eye gaze in real-time at a low cost, with low power consumption, and with robustness to a wide variety of illumination conditions.

we have designed and implemented a system that enables graceful degradation across the spectrum of illumination, from indoor office lighting to outdoor sunlight, and that can operate at a low-power rate of 7mW, or at a high-power rate of 32mW, while still achieving high accuracy in estimating eye parameters.

we have designed a system for continuous, non-invasive eye tracking that can be operated in a power-efficient manner under indoor lighting, and that gracefully transitions to a robust mode under outdoor lighting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we present a staged architecture for a wearable eye tracker that can operate at high rates with robustness across the spectrum of illumination conditions, while consuming low power.
our staged architecture enables graceful degradation in performance as the environment changes from indoor to outdoor settings.
our staged architecture enables a power-robustness tradeoff that is not possible with a single model, and that our system design enables a wearable eye tracker to run on a computational eyeglass.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a) a staged design can enable robustness-power tradeoffs in wearable systems, b) the use of a fast search-refine controller enables low-power operation under indoor settings, and c) the use of an adaptive controller can enable graceful adaptation to more challenging outdoor settings.

we can design a wearable system that is robust to the wide spectrum of illumination in the natural environment, but also operates at a power consumption that is an order of magnitude less than the state-of-the-art.
we can achieve a robustness--power tradeoff that enables the design of a low-power eye tracker that operates under a wide spectrum of lighting conditions.
